claim: Claims its value of $540,000 from the defendant management company for the stolen car
requested_remedy: Claims its value of $540,000 from the defendant management company for the stolen car
parties: Defendant: The management company of Scenic Villas

facts.F1: Mr Henry Ching's Toyota Lexus was stolen from the carpark of Scenic Villas on the night of 19 November 1991.
facts.F2: The thief or thieves entered the carpark in a stolen Honda, circumvented the sophisticated Lexus alarm system in less than 20 minutes, and departed in the Lexus.
facts.F3: The elderly caretaker, who was on duty that night, made two signed statements about the incident but has since disappeared.
facts.F4: Mr Ching is the general manager of the plaintiff, the Reebok Company Limited, and was provided with the car and an apartment at Scenic Villas as part of his employment.
facts.F5: Scenic Villas has one road access for vehicles and a night caretaker who operates the barrier arms with a button.
facts.F6: Around 1990/1991, there was a sudden and notorious upsurge of vehicle thefts in Hong Kong, with luxury model cars being targeted by thieves.
facts.F7: Scenic Villas carpark was no exception, with four cars stolen in just over one year, including Mr Ching's previous company car, a Toyota Crown.
facts.F8: The defendant management company had taken some security measures, including a patrolling system, beatbooks, and 'walkie-talkies' for caretakers.
facts.F9: The defendant had also recommended and obtained a quotation for a special carpark access control system, but it was not implemented due to an objection from one of the owners.
facts.F10: The caretaker had been instructed to record registration numbers, look at drivers' faces, and question them if appropriate.
facts.F11: The plaintiff's car was on a list of 10 high-risk or luxury models that the caretaker had been warned about.
facts.F12: The caretaker had raised the barrier and let the stolen Lexus drive away after the driver had given a flat number that matched the one on the Lexus' windscreen label.
facts.F13: The caretaker had later gone to Mr Ching's flat to 'double-check' and had reported the theft to the police immediately.
facts.F14: The supermarket within Scenic Villas is open to the public until late hours and has customers who are not residents, which affects the defendant's control over vehicles and their occupants.
facts.F15: The defendant had taken reasonable steps to address the risk of vehicle theft.
facts.F16: The caretaker's actions on the night of the theft were in line with the defendant's instructions and policies, except for a lapse that did not cause the loss of the car.

claim: The plaintiff is claiming damages for injuries sustained from being knocked down by a motorcycle in July 1975.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff is claiming damages for injuries sustained from being knocked down by a motorcycle in July 1975.

facts.F1: The plaintiff was fifty-seven years of age and worked as a waitress in a small restaurant at the time of the accident.
facts.F2: The plaintiff was detained in hospital for some nine months after the accident.
facts.F3: The plaintiff spent three months with one or both legs in traction and most of the remainder with the right leg in plaster.
facts.F4: The plaintiff received treatment and instruction in physiotherapy in the last three weeks of her hospital stay.
facts.F5: A medical report dated July 1976 indicated that the first three items of injury mentioned above have left no permanent disability.
facts.F6: The medical report also showed that there was considerable restriction in the movements of the right arm and both legs; shortening of both legs, and to different degrees; wastage of various muscles; several small scars, one of which had been remedied to some extent by a skin graft; and a substantial loss of grip strength in the right arm.
facts.F7: The plaintiff walked with a shuffling gait, could do so only slowly and for about one hour at a time and had difficulty in climbing steps.
facts.F8: The plaintiff was unfit for any form of work which involved standing or walking and was unable to lift heavy weights.
facts.F9: The doctor assessed her impairment as 15 per cent of the whole woman.
facts.F10: The plaintiff started work again for her previous employer on the 1st January that year, doing much lighter work at the reduced salary of $400 per month.
facts.F11: The plaintiff's husband spent $5,000 on providing extra nourishment to her during her recovery, but this was not recoverable as the plaintiff did not incur the expense herself.
facts.F12: The assessment of general damages was based on the plaintiff's pain and suffering, loss of amenities, and loss of future earnings.
facts.F13: The special damages were based on the plaintiff's loss of past earnings, travelling expenses, and other expenses directly related to her recovery from the injury, but not including expenses incurred by her husband.

facts.F1: Luckson Ltd and Shing Yip Ltd are companies incorporated in the British Virgin Islands, registered as having a place of business in Hong Kong under part XI of the Companies Ordinance.
facts.F2: The Petitioner and the Respondents are the only shareholders, each holding one-third of the shares in each company.
facts.F3: The BVI companies hold the entire share capital of two Hong Kong companies, Ever Rich (Group) Ltd and Ever Rich Printing Manufacturing Company Ltd.
facts.F4: The Hong Kong companies are the main assets of the BVI companies.
facts.F5: The Petitioner alleges that prior to the incorporation of the BVI companies in about 1996, he and the Respondents were equal shareholders in the Hong Kong companies, which were run by them as a quasi-partnership.
facts.F6: The Petitioner claims that the BVI companies were incorporated at the suggestion of the Respondents, who assured him that after their incorporation and the transfer to them of the Petitioner’s and the Respondents' shareholdings of the Hong Kong companies, all the companies would continue to be run on the same basis.
facts.F7: The Petitioner alleges that the relationship between the Respondents and himself broke down towards the end of 2001.
facts.F8: The Petitioner alleges that at a time when it was proposed that Ever Rich (Group) Ltd should be listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, the proposed financial advisers for the listing application, Messrs Deloitte, discovered irregularities and inconsistencies in its financial records.
facts.F9: The Petitioner alleges that there followed between December 2001 and March 2002 a series of steps which had the effect of excluding him from the management of the Hong Kong and BVI companies, culminating on 7 March 2002 with the passing of resolutions removing him as a director of the BVI companies.
facts.F10: On 8 March 2002, the Petitioner issued proceedings against the Respondents, the Hong Kong companies, and the BVI companies, seeking orders requiring them to reinstate him as a director of the BVI companies and to restore him to the management of the Hong Kong companies.
facts.F11: On 17 July 2002, the Respondents were appointed as additional directors of the Hong Kong companies.
facts.F12: On 25 October 2002, the Petitioner took out his application for the appointment of provisional liquidators in respect of the BVI companies.
facts.F13: The Respondents, as representatives of the BVI companies, made declarations of solvency in respect of the Hong Kong companies on 29 October 2002, and passed special resolutions for the voluntary winding up of the Hong Kong companies on 4 November 2002.
facts.F14: Messrs Lai Kar Yan Derek and Darach E Haughey, partners of Deloitte, were appointed liquidators of the Hong Kong companies.
facts.F15: The liquidators of the Hong Kong companies would be aware of the Petitions and the outstanding action, and the allegations made in them, and would have to look into these matters and take such action as they may think appropriate.
facts.F16: The costs of appointing a provisional liquidator would be increased if someone other than Messrs Lai and Haughey were to be appointed.
